prime.problem: Binomial tails ("at least 50 of 100 customers wait over 10 minutes") are sums of many terms. By hand, and for quick reasoning, you approximate them with a normal, but cutting at the wrong place loses a whole half-bar and makes the answer 35% low.
prime.fits: It's the CLT card applied to a count of 0/1 trials, with one extra rule for whole numbers. The probability p = e<sup>−1</sup> comes from the exponential card's pharmacy, and the sample-size card reuses the same normal machinery.
expect: Bin(n, p) as a sum of 0/1 trials
prime.goal: Approximate any binomial tail with the corrected normal, know which way to shift the cut for ≥, >, ≤ and <, and know when to sum exactly instead.

attend: Why does each customer wait over 10 minutes with chance e<sup>−1</sup>, and which card supplies that?
Why is the right cut 49.5 for "at least 50", and what share of the answer does the 50 bar alone carry?
Why does the Poisson(np) approximation overshoot by 4.7× here?
Why does even the corrected normal drift low further into the tail?

must: A binomial count is a sum of n independent 0/1 trials → by the CLT its bars follow a normal with mean np and variance np(1 − p) → 36.79 and 23.25 (sd 4.822) for the pharmacy
Bars are one unit wide and bar k covers k − ½ to k + ½ → "at least 50" starts at 49.5 → cutting at 50 drops half the 50 bar (0.00213 of a 0.0047 answer) → 35% low without the ½, 11% low with it

The normal matches mean and variance but not the skew → accurate in the middle (within 1% at k = 35, 40) and increasingly low in the far tail (0.75× at k = 55) → with a computer, sum the exact tail with math.comb
elevated: Poisson(np) uses variance np, not np(1 − p) → too wide when p isn't small (p = 0.37 here) → 0.0219, 4.7× the exact 0.004708 → Poisson only for rare events
reference: the rule of thumb np, n(1 − p) ≥ 10 (some texts use 5)
de Moivre–Laplace as the theorem's name

compress.prompt: From memory, draw three bars around 50 with the normal curve over them and mark where the cut goes for "at least 50". Then write the full calculation in two lines and one line on when you'd skip the approximation.
checklist: ≥ k and < k cut at k − ½; ≤ k and > k cut at k + ½
exact 0.004708: the normal is good in the middle, low in the far tail
with a computer, sum the binomial exactly

retrieve.q: Explain the continuity correction to someone who knows the CLT but not this rule, using the bar picture.
answer: the binomial puts mass on whole numbers; each bar is one unit wide
the normal is a smooth area, so "bars 50 and up" is the area from the left edge of bar 50, 49.5
cutting at 50 misses half of bar 50

retrieve.q: Walk through P(X ≤ 30) for the same Bin(100, e<sup>−1</sup>): where you cut, the z-score, and how the result compares with the exact sum.
answer: ≤ 30 includes all of bar 30, so cut at 30.5
exact 0.0948; without the ½ you'd get 0.0796

retrieve.q: You have a laptop and need P(at least 50 of 100). Normal with ½, Poisson, Cantelli, or exact sum: which do you report, and when would each of the others still be the right call?
answer: report the exact sum: 51 terms, microseconds
normal with ½: exams and mental checks ("2.6 sd up, well under 1%")
Poisson: when p is small and n large
Cantelli: only when you need a guarantee with no shape assumption

compare.q: This card is the CLT for a count. What does a count need that A.J.'s job times didn't, and why?
answer: a count takes only whole values, so its mass sits on bars
the normal area must be matched to whole bars, hence the ±½
job times are continuous, so no correction is needed there

compare.q: cs-8 computed binomial probabilities exactly. When is the exact binomial still the right choice, and what does the normal buy you?
answer: exact whenever you can compute it: it's always correct and cheap with math.comb
the normal buys a formula you can reason with (z-scores) and do by hand
and it generalises to other sums where no exact law is known

predict.q: Keep n = 100 but make each customer wait over 10 minutes with p = 0.5. Before computing: is the corrected normal more or less accurate for P(X ≥ 60) than it was for the pharmacy's P(X ≥ 50), and why?
predict.answer: More accurate. With p = 0.5 the binomial is exactly symmetric (skewness (1 − 2p)/σ = 0), so the normal's only error is the discreteness, which the ½ handles. 60 is 1.9 sd above the mean 50 (sd 5), less far out than the pharmacy's 2.6 sd, which helps too.

apply.task: Use the card's functions to print, for Bin(100, e−1), the exact P(X ≤ 30), the normal with the cut at 30.5 and the normal cut at 30. Then write a helper cut(k, kind) that returns k − ½ or k + ½ for the four kinds ≥, >, ≤, < and test it on k = 30.
apply.done: You print 0.0948 (exact), 0.0961 (cut 30.5) and 0.0796 (cut 30), and your helper returns 29.5, 30.5, 30.5, 29.5 for ≥, >, ≤, <.
apply.hint: The cut sits at the edge of the last bar you include (or the first you exclude).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the p = 0.5 accuracy, or the reason?
Could you explain why the correction shifts left for ≥ and right for ≤?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: sum of 0/1 trials → normal, or unit-wide bars → ±½?
When did you last approximate a count with a normal without correcting it?
What will you revisit before the sample-size card: how the normal's z turns into a required n?
